newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain's Major embattled at EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major embattled at EU summit.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, slipping further behind in opinion polls as an election approaches, plunged into another rumpus over Europe on Saturday.
Major flew into Dublin to warn his fellow leaders at a European Union summit of the dangers of being too radical in overhauling the way the bloc works.
"Look before you leap is a far better watchword for Europe than leap before you look," Major said after the talks.

But his message, designed to set the tone for next week's Conservative conference and prevent a renewed bout of party infighting Europe, was overshadowed by a scathing attack on Major by the president of the European Parliament.

In an eve-of-summit speech, Klaus Haensch accused Britain of being out of step with Europe and of "blackmail tactics" over the mad cow crisis. He warned the rest of Europe would not hold up reform for Britain.
"I fail to see why 14 governments should always have to sacrifice their vision of Europe, and their principles, to keep on board a government which may jump ship in any case.

"If one government is clearly out of step with the 14 others... then the others may have to look at ways of moving forward nonetheless or of postponing final decisions until the government in the minority is prepared to change its position, or until another takes its place," Haensch said.

Major, already angry that the leaders of Portugal, Austria and the Netherlands sent videos to last week's Labour party conference backing his rival, opposition leader Tony Blair, was furious. Aides decribed him as "hopping mad".

Major complained strongly to summit host, Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, and updbraided Haensch in front of other leaders, saying the socialist head of Europe's parliament did not understand Britain's position, aides said.

"The British are good Europeans," Major said at his news conference. Asked to confirm he had criticised Haensch publicly, Major added: "Yes I did. I told him his remarks were offensive... I think the points I made to him had some impact."
Major had hoped for a quiet summit ahead of his crucial party conference, the last before the general election now no more than seven months away.
But the spat with Haensch once again underlined how Major's attempts to keep quiet the Eurosceptics in his party has eroded his influence in Europe.

As Major left early to prepare for an eve-of-conference television interview in London, the other leaders reaffirmed that the final decision on the treaty they are preparing to overhaul the European Union's workings will be taken in June.
The last date Major can call the election is in May and polls on Saturday and Sunday confirmed Major has an electoral mountain to climb before then.
A Gallup poll in Saturday's Daily Telegraph said Blair's lead soared from 24.5 to 33 points after last week's conference and the eruption of a new row over government sleaze.
An NOP poll for the Sunday Times also showed a four point jump in Blair's lead in the last two weeks to 23 points.
